rounds.proof_sketch: Grid is launched with dim3 grid(..., N) where N=16. CUDA blockIdx.z ranges from 0 to grid.z-1, i.e., bz ∈ [0, 15]. Original guard 'bz >= N' triggers when bz >= 16 (never true). Mutated guard 'bz > N' triggers when bz > 16 (also never true). The only distinguishing case bz == 16 is unreachable since max(bz) = 15.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes the early-exit guard from 'bz >= N' to 'bz > N'. For this to produce different behavior, there must exist a thread block where bz == N exactly. However, the kernel launch configures grid.z = N (the batch size, which is 16 in this fixed configuration). CUDA thread blocks have blockIdx.z ranging from 0 to grid.z-1, meaning bz ∈ [0, N-1] = [0, 15]. Since bz can never equal N=16, both the original and mutated guards evaluate to false for all thread blocks. The guard was essentially dead code in the original (providing safety for hypothetical misconfigurations), and the mutation preserves this behavior under the fixed shape contract.
rounds.kill_strategy: Unkillable under fixed-shape contract. The mutation affects a boundary guard whose triggering condition (bz == N) is architecturally impossible when grid.z equals N. Killing this mutant would require changing the batch dimension N or the grid launch configuration, both of which are shape-dependent and fixed.
rounds.recommendations: For mutation testing of CUDA kernels, boundary guards that depend on launch configuration (grid dimensions) rather than runtime values are often unkillable under fixed-shape contracts. Consider either: (1) marking such guards as equivalent mutations during test design, or (2) including shape variation as a required testing dimension for comprehensive kernel correctness validation.
